title: Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) Guidelines, 01 May 2026 (Tactical Field Care: Tourniquet Reassessment)
org: Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC), Joint Trauma System, US Department of Defense (published on Deployed Medicine)
licence_note: US Department of Defense work. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: limb tourniquets converted to hemostatic or pressure dressings as soon as possible if three criteria are met (not in shock; wound can be watched closely; not an amputation); every effort to convert in less than 2 hours if bleeding can be controlled by other means; do not remove a tourniquet in place more than 6 hours unless close monitoring and lab capability are available; ASM/CLS-trained personnel should not convert beyond 2 hours without medical direction.

title: Prolonged Casualty Care Guidelines (Clinical Practice Guideline ID 91), 21 December 2021
org: Joint Trauma System, US Department of Defense
licence_note: US Department of Defense work. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16 (Deployed Medicine copy of the JTS PDF): check tourniquets have not shifted or loosened; consider tourniquet conversion (more than 2 hours but before 6 hours) at Role 1b; convert per TCCC guidelines in less than 2 hours if bleeding can be controlled by other means; DO NOT remove a tourniquet in place more than 6 hours; do not remove a tourniquet to relieve pain; re-check all pulses after splint placement.

title: TCCC Combat Medic/Corpsman Skill Instructions: Tourniquet Conversion (TCCC-CMC-09-01, 23 Jan 2021)
org: Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC), Joint Trauma System, US Department of Defense
licence_note: US Department of Defense work. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: condition (non-amputated limb, not in shock, wound amenable to dressing and/or extended evacuation expected); pack the wound, firm pressure at least 3 minutes, pressure bandage, release the tourniquet slowly over one minute while watching the bandage; convert in less than 2 hours if possible, do not remove one in place more than 6 hours; if bleeding recurs, retighten the original tourniquet until bleeding is controlled and the distal pulse is absent.

title: Minimum Guidelines and Scope of Practice for Wilderness First Aid (version of 14 December 2012; published in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine 2013;24(4):456-62)
org: Wilderness First Aid writing group (Johnson DE, Schimelpfenig T and others), published in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine, journal of the Wilderness Medical Society
licence_note: Copyright the writing group and the journal publisher. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16 (the writing group's Dec 2012 PDF): treat unstable injuries with gentle traction into position for angulated long bones; traction into position for joints only if circulation, sensation and movement are impaired or splinting in position is impossible; splints that allow ongoing monitoring of perfusion. WFA scope does not include releasing tourniquets placed to control life-threatening bleeding.

title: Broken bone (first aid)
org: MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine / NIH)
licence_note: MedlinePlus encyclopedia text licensed from A.D.A.M.; review date 1/14/2026. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: signs of poor circulation (pale or blue skin, numbness or tingling, loss of pulse); if circulation is poor and trained personnel are NOT quickly available, try to realign the limb into a normal resting position; DO NOT attempt to straighten a bone unless circulation appears hampered and no medically trained personnel are nearby; never reposition a suspected spine injury.

title: How to Safely Handle and Store Eggs from Your Home Flock (updated September 12, 2024)
licence_note: Copyright The Pennsylvania State University. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: water glassing is not recommended; the shell membrane lets water and pathogens pass; a home pantry or basement will not hold 40 °F or below; recommended alternatives are refrigeration, freezing out of the shell, refrigerated pickled eggs and freeze-drying.

title: Storing Eggs Safely (You Asked It!, November 13, 2020)
org: Kansas State University Research and Extension, Rapid Response Center
licence_note: Copyright Kansas State University. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: storing eggs in lime water is not recommended; Salmonella enteritidis can be inside the egg before it is laid; small home flocks have a higher incidence; lime water could seep through the shell; refrigeration is best for safety and quality.

title: Freezing Eggs
org: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia)
licence_note: Copyright National Center for Home Food Preservation. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: eggs keep at least 1 month covered in the refrigerator; freeze out of the shell, each egg broken separately and examined; whole eggs mixed (not whipped) with sugar, corn syrup or salt against graininess, 1/2-inch headspace.

title: What You Need to Know About Egg Safety (content current as of 03/05/2024)
licence_note: US federal government work. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: clean uncracked eggs may contain Salmonella; symptoms 12 to 72 hours after infection; children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems at greater risk; refrigerate at 40 °F or below; cook until yolk and white are firm; egg dishes to 160 °F.

title: Residential Gas Water Heaters Instruction Manual (part no. 196293-002), lighting instructions label 'For your safety read before lighting'
licence_note: Manufacturer manual, copyright A. O. Smith. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: before lighting, smell all around the appliance and next to the floor; what to do if you smell gas (do not light, no switches or phones, call the gas supplier from a neighbour's phone); turn the knob by hand only, never tools; do not use if any part has been under water; turn to OFF, wait five minutes to clear gas, smell again, then light the pilot per the steps; if the pilot will not stay lit, turn off and call a technician.

title: Important Propane Safety Information (brochure PRC 003121, 2005), as distributed by the Mississippi State Fire Marshal
licence_note: Copyright Propane Education & Research Council. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: if you smell gas, no flames or sparks, leave, shut off the tank valve if safe, report from a neighbour's home, do not return until the retailer says it is safe; running out of gas puts pilots out and an open valve can leak when the system is recharged; a leak check is required in many states before turning on the gas; strongly recommended that only a qualified service technician light a pilot that has gone out; lighting it yourself risks fire or explosion; follow the manufacturer's instructions.

title: Home Safe Home: Propane Safety Tips for the Home
org: Railroad Commission of Texas (state propane regulator)
licence_note: State agency publication. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: never light a pilot if you smell gas; if gas smell continues after lighting, close the appliance valve and call the supplier; in most situations best to have a trained technician light pilots; a flooded gas control must be replaced; after a leak, a technician checks all appliances and relights pilots.

title: The "Invisible" Killer: Carbon Monoxide (CPSC Publication 464)
licence_note: US federal government work. Read by L6 on 2026-11-16: always follow the appliance manufacturer's directions for safe operation; have heating systems inspected annually by a trained technician; signs of improper operation (sooting, unfamiliar or burning odour, moisture on windows); only a trained technician can detect hidden problems such as improper burner adjustment or hidden chimney blockage; CO alarms near sleeping areas.
